lektioner.sammanfattning: Sales/motivation intro: leverage of making ads vs editing, the six pillars of the course, and that ad creation is normally split between a creative strategist, a copywriter and an editor.
Explains CPM, CTR, conversion rate, ROAS and CPA with a $100 example, and states that ads must run 3-7 days (about a week) before being judged winners or losers unless obviously burning money.

Why raw, authentic 'ugly' ads beat polished production (pattern interrupt, authenticity, relatability); direct response is measurable and gives instant feedback; test both styles and let the data guide you; you cannot just throw random ads out.
Build a detailed customer avatar from research; spend 80% of time on understanding the customer and 20% on the edit. Nothing on volume or funnel.
Desire cannot be created, only channelled; every product is a physical product plus a transformational product; show the desire being fulfilled rather than claiming it. Nothing on volume or funnel.

The agency process: research, brainstorming, strategy, copywriting, production, testing, iteration. Media buyer pushes spend into ads that work and turns off ads that do not; iteration means analysing why winners worked to replicate them and why losers failed to avoid the mistakes.

Three sources of ad ideas: old advertising books, organic social media research plus comment mining, and ad spy tools (Atria). Warns that copying competitor ads makes you second best; long-running ads in Atria usually indicate profitability.
Intro to the video ads pillar: organic, UGC, high production and VSL formats, and the story of a cinematic production flopping while a raw iPhone ASMR video won.

Three organic video-ad styles (customer testimonials, social-media-style, lifestyle) chosen by what the customer already consumes; the ad must not look like an ad, copy sounds like a person not a brand. Editing is deliberately minimal.
Walkthrough of three organic briefs. Establishes the course's standard unit: one concept = one 'hold' (body) plus three variations that differ only in the hook text (or the comment-reply hook).

Defines UGC as strategic, persuasion-driven creator content; gives the hook / problem / twist-the-knife / product / feature-benefit / bad-alternative / results / CTA structure and the five-step production process (research, ideation, script, production, editing). Contains the only uses of the word root 'intent' in this part (intentional/intentionally), meaning deliberate sourcing of creators, not purchase intent.
Three UGC briefs. Variations again differ only by the hook; when only one hook line exists, the three variations use three different hook visuals instead of three hook texts.

Video sales letters (1-15+ minutes) for education-heavy, problem-solving, older-audience products; four elements (hook, problem amplification, hope spot, solution buildup) and how to edit them (audio first, b-roll, captions, animate only key points).

Two VSL briefs: one with three hooks and three matching CTAs exported as three ads, one where the 'hooks' are completely different leads/angles into the same body. Notes that an agency edit the client loved 'didn't perform that well'.

When premium production is worth it (premium price point, visual products, long-game brands). Describes the multi-touch customer journey where organic/UGC gets first attention and premium assets convince later; premium footage becomes a reusable b-roll library.
A 10-15 second three-step studio ad brief for a shilajit brand; colour-grade raw footage and add on-screen text.

What makes a visual hook work (composition, context, hook text from frame one), then the course's testing doctrine: never run one version, test messaging and visuals separately in sets of three, use the winner as the new baseline and test the next three against it, let data not gut decide, and test even 'dumb' ideas.

Retention principles for video ads: stack open loops before revealing the product, keep visual variety every 1-3 seconds matched to the audience's age, and use progress bars/timers to hold viewers to the end. Nothing on testing volume, spend, iteration or funnel stages.

Technical lesson on Meta placements (feed, stories, reels) and keeping text, captions and product inside a safe-zone overlay so one 9:16 export works everywhere; 4:5 as the alternative for horizontal footage. Not relevant to the question.

Keep all client content locally on an SSD, organized per brand into UGC, product shots, high production, ad concepts, hooks, and per creator. Only marginal relevance: content from creators whose ads perform better should be used more.

How sound effects support visuals and how music pauses build tension (Dr. Squatch, a protein brand, a humidifier ad). One aside: the agency found heavy-SFX edited ads 'just don't work for us', an example of processing a learning; otherwise not relevant.

lektioner.titel: My Tech Stack For Editing Video Ads (30:21)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Editing software, plugins, footage sources (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Envato, Pexels, Artlist), music sourcing, and inspiration (team inspo channel, Atria, Meta Ad Library). Frames volume as 'reps' that build editor skill, not as a function of spend. Not relevant to the intent question.
Intro loom: the following breakdown videos show the presenter and agency editors editing ads from scratch and applying marketing/psychological principles. No relevant content.

lektioner.titel: LIVE Example: Editing a Video Ad (54:02)
lektioner.sammanfattning: A live editing walkthrough of a UGC testimonial ad for a ceramic coffee cup (Stoke): edit by layers (A-roll/VO, music, B-roll, animations, captions, SFX), green-screen technique, B-roll sourcing from TikTok/Pinterest/brand Instagram, and organic TikTok-style captions. Only indirect relevance: the editor mentions the old volume pace (5-6 concepts a day, 3 variations each) and that a script carries three hooks cut into separate variations.

An agency editor breaks down a dog-harness ad from brief to voiceover: reading the brief (9:16, three hooks, one body, three total ads), folder structure, generating and regenerating ElevenLabs voiceover, volume levels, removing pauses and inhales in Premiere Pro. Only relevance is the brief spec of three hooks per body and average video length.

Editor walks through music selection for a dog-harness organic-style ad: screenshotting the brief into ChatGPT for search phrases, browsing Artlist/Extreme Music, then mixing voice over music with a parametric EQ preset and volume adjustments. Nothing about testing volume, spend, retargeting or intent.

Editor finishes the same ad clip by clip from the brief (creator footage, TikTok stock clips, text-overlay removal, After Effects arrow tracking, captions, hook text), then produces H2 and H3 by duplicating the finished sequence and reworking only the hook. Only marginally relevant: it shows the 3-hooks-per-video variation structure and that the ad is built as a 'same idea as the reference winner, done differently' iteration.

An editor at the agency walks through editing a UGC ad (Metaglow collagen) in Premiere Pro: brief reading, folder setup, A-roll cutting, audio compression, B-roll, captions, hook text, and exporting. Only tangentially relevant: it shows that a batch is one hold with three hook variations, and that variations are made by swapping only the hook text.

Editing breakdown of an organic-style ad for Dog Friendly Co: ElevenLabs AI voiceover, music sourcing, split-screen B-roll, hooks and captions. Tangentially relevant: one concept (negative framing) per batch with three hooks that piggyback on the same idea, the hook is the vital lever, and editing choices are driven by learnings from top-spending ads.

Editor walks through a text-only organic ad for a dog harness: music first, cut text on the beat, source B-roll from TikTok, keep animations minimal. The only strategy content is the opening: the brief was built by combining an under-spent ad with potential and a well-performing UGC ad, and hook 2 reuses the UGC ad's winning hook.

Editor breaks down a long VSL for Flow Pouches (mushroom pouches): B-roll planning table, AI voiceover cleanup, music remixing, stock footage, After Effects framing, captions and sound effects. Pure editing tutorial; only mentions that the brief has three hooks and one hold and that most spend goes to men in their late twenties and above.

Six principles for static ads: instant impact of one frame, old-school copy principles (market sophistication, Ogilvy headlines), five static-ad types mapped to the audience's main objection (product-focused for retargeting/price, transformation for 'does it work', lifestyle, problem-solution, testimonial for trust), headline triggers, visual hierarchy, and 'just do reps'. Says to test types against each other and that statics let you iterate faster than video.
Technical placement rule: in 9x16 statics keep everything inside a 1080x1080 safe zone because feed crops to 1x1. No testing or funnel content.

lektioner.titel: My Tech Stack For Doing Static Ads + Workflow (15:23)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Figma + Photoshop tooling and the Figma file structure: one frame per brand, ad concepts numbered, and three variations (V1, V2, V3) per ad concept before moving to the next concept. Statics need no footage so they are fast to produce.
Walkthrough of a 700+ template Figma library and a live testimonial ad build for Carapod in under 10 minutes; point is that statics can be cranked out very fast.
Five static-ad briefs for students; the us-vs-them brief specifies three variations where everything is identical except the single review/comment on the product side.
Using Topaz Gigapixel / Video AI to upscale low-quality images and footage. Pure tooling.
Intro to the AI product-image methods (PhotoRoom/Flair, Midjourney, trained models) for generating product visuals without a studio shoot. Tooling only.

Two methods for AI product images with client examples; notes that the shown statics got a lot of spend and scaled accounts, and that an 'okay' performing ad became a winner after an AI-visual iteration.

lektioner.titel: AI Product Images - Method 1 (Easy / Okay Results) (8:38)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Loom on Photoshop generative fill and PhotoRoom backgrounds for a product PNG. Tooling only.

lektioner.titel: AI Product Images - Method 2 (Medium / Great Results) (14:18)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Step-by-step Midjourney + Photoshop tutorial for generating a static product image (Nurgit shilajit jar on a bedside table): Pinterest reference images, /describe, prompt building, upscaling, product overlay, lighting with color dodge, overlay filter. Opens with the creative idea: a new 'sleep insurance' mechanism tested with two headlines.

lektioner.titel: AI Product Images - Method 2.1 (Medium / Great Results) (7:06)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Same Midjourney method applied to a jewelry brand (Cali Tiger): reference image + product image, /describe keywords, vary-region tool, repeated generations until the product matches. Pure image-generation tutorial.

lektioner.titel: AI Product Images - Method 3 (Medium / Best Results) (Must Watch) (15:39)
lektioner.sammanfattning: fal.ai tutorial: train a custom Flux LoRA on 6-15+ product images (trigger word, ~1000 steps) and then generate unlimited product scenes from text prompts, optionally written by Claude/ChatGPT. Pay-per-use pricing (~29 images per $1). No media-buying content.

lektioner.titel: iPhone Image > AI High-Production Image > AI High-Production Video (24:37)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Live walkthrough: Midjourney scene -> Photoshop product compositing -> Luma Labs image-to-video -> speed ramp in Final Cut -> Topaz upscale/slow-motion, to get 'unlimited' high-production product images and videos from an iPhone photo. Pure production tutorial.

ElevenLabs tutorial: library voices, instant voice clone, Studio with one chapter per hook (hook 1/2/3 + hold + CTA), formatting tricks (caps, commas, dashes, exclamation marks, 'and/so') so the voiceover sounds human. Framed around an ad on pace to become a top spender made from AI voiceover + product b-roll only, and around replicating a winning creator ad by cloning her voice.

Arcads tutorial for AI UGC avatars: format the script with BreakTime so three hooks fit in one generation ('we always test three variations for each of our ads'), pick avatars that look like the target demographic, cover weak lip-sync with b-roll. Emphasises speed: an ad in an hour or two instead of a week with a creator.

Tool walkthrough of HeyGen: a creator records a 2-5 minute clip holding the product, an avatar is trained on it, and unlimited scripts can then be generated with lip-sync; also stock UGC/professional avatars.
Unpublished placeholder, no content.

Defines creative strategy and lays out the agency workflow: onboarding form, AI market research, ad-account audit of winners, content audit, the Growth Guide sheet (batch number, concept, avatar, desire, awareness level, hypothesis, ad type iteration/imitation/ideation, format, result, learnings, winning-ad hit rate), AI ad review checklist before testing, and closing the feedback loop after 5-10 days on every ad.

Schwartz's five awareness levels (unaware to most aware), what ads work at each level, and that an ad must walk the customer through every remaining level; offer/discount-only ads only work for the most-aware, and cracking an unaware ad opens a new market.

Umbrella story for Schwartz's five sophistication stages: plain claim, bigger claim, new mechanism, mechanism fatigue, then reimagine via identity/values or a niche; alternative solutions to the same problem also raise sophistication, so advertising must keep changing approach as competition grows.

lektioner.titel: How To Do Deep Market Research (With AI) (1:11:06)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Walkthrough of a 14-page market-research prompt (brand/product analysis, desire and problem mapping, competitor research, Amazon/Reddit/social-media mining, hook and objection analysis, market-sophistication level, ad-concept recommendations) using a mushroom-pouch brand as example. The point is that ads should come from a systemized research process (awareness levels + market sophistication) rather than random spam testing; it says nothing about ad volume, spend thresholds, retargeting or iteration ratios.

lektioner.titel: How To Give Claude Access To Browse The Internet (9:03)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Technical setup tutorial: install Claude Desktop, Node.js, Brave Search API key and an MCP config so Claude can search the web for research. No content on creative volume, funnel stages or testing.

Setting up a Claude project per brand: ad-account audit (top performers plus the graveyard of losers), content audit, comment mining of top ads, transcribing the top 3 ads, then generating five target avatars and 10 mass desires from the knowledge base. Workflow/setup lesson, almost nothing on volume, retargeting or scaling.

The growth guide spreadsheet tracks every ad concept by avatar, desire, awareness level and learning. Core message: random spam-testing of creatives cannot scale a brand; if 20 concepts produce no winner you are structurally wrong and must change avatar/desire/awareness level, not just make more ads.

Three idea sources are iteration, imitation and ideation; imitations (ripping competitor ads) are the easiest to make but have produced the fewest winners. Shows how a concept is entered in the growth guide with 2-3 headline/desire variations, tested, then judged winner/loser with learnings logged; weekly one-hour strategy block per brand; shares as a signal of winning ads.

How to come up with net-new ad concepts: study the market research document, analyze existing winning ads and content, mine reviews/comments with Claude, TikTok/Reddit/AnswerThePublic research. States that most winning ads come from fresh ideation (the hardest work) and shows how a line from a winning video became a new static concept that was then iterated on.

Iterate only on ads that are performing well or showing potential: new hooks, new creator, same concept as static/VSL/organic, doubling down on the winning headline/angle. Shows a 3-variation static test where one won and two did nothing, and the learnings taken. Iterations are the easy part; finding the first thing that works is the hard part.

lektioner.titel: How To Write Copy For Static Ads (With AI) (23:57)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Walkthrough of a 14-page Claude prompt for static-ad headlines inside a brand project. Repeatedly stresses the prompt only works if you did the research and have a good idea; AI is a speed tool for pumping out statics, not a replacement for judgement about which headlines fit the customer.

lektioner.titel: How To Write Scripts For Video Ads (With AI) (23:48)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Same prompt workflow for video scripts with three types (general, organic, storytelling); the prompt returns six hooks, one script and a strategic breakdown. Warns explicitly against spam-testing creatives without understanding them and argues for human input over full automation; scripts are ~80% there and need adjustment.

lektioner.titel: Prompt Engineering (How to communicate with AI) (33:56)
lektioner.sammanfattning: How the course's 15-page ad-writing prompts are built (purpose, step-by-step process, mini knowledge base, examples, web research) and a prediction of an agent workflow: ideation agent -> script agent -> design/editing agent -> media-buying agent -> review agent that waits 5-7 days, judges ads on spend/ROAS/purchases and feeds learnings back. Stresses that human marketing expertise must sit on top; the course itself is NOT fully automating.

Every ad, winner or loser, must get processed learnings (weekly team learnings call). Worked example: 3 static variations of one concept, the top spender is dissected per variable (background, headline, callouts, CTR), losers are diagnosed, and the next batch is 3 new variations built around the winning headline plus fixes. Metrics list and a question checklist for reviewing ads.

Breakdown of an unaware dog-harness ad: idea came from a 178-page market research document (adoption + pulling), a viral TikTok as swipe, a brief with three hooks, AI-written script with strategic breakdown. One of the first ads made became top spender in almost all campaigns within ~30 days; editing played the smallest role.

Start of the CarePod humidifier ad breakdown: existing creator/organic content library repurposed with an AI voiceover into a native-looking Instagram-style ad. Cut off mid-lesson in this chunk (continues in the next part).

lektioner.titel: How I Turned A Losing Ad Into A Winning Ad (55:42)
lektioner.sammanfattning: Walkthrough of processing learnings on an ad that was top spender for seven days and then died, then rewriting it (same structure, more persuasion, later product intro, text-on-screen format) into a winner. Core message: a spent-but-not-quite ad is a source of new winners if you close the feedback loop; AI is a tool, not the strategist.

Presentation on conscious vs unconscious mind and a four-phase creative process (feed the brain, incubate, capture, develop). Argues that forcing volume of ad ideas on demand produces nothing that wins; research input is what can be forced, not creative output.

lektioner.titel: How I Approach Research/Coming Up With Ad Ideas (11:19)
lektioner.sammanfattning: A workflow lesson about capturing ad ideas throughout the week with the MyMind app (auto-tagging notes, bookmarks, swipes), then turning a captured idea into an ad concept in the growth guide during a weekly two-hour Thursday strategy call by mapping it to avatar, mass desire, awareness stage and format. Almost entirely about idea capture tooling; only marginally relevant to volume-vs-intent.

Live call where the FunPunch co-founder (Pavel) and the course leads (Karlo/Lowro) walk through the brand's top-spending ads, explain why each one works (visual TOF rhythm ads, sound-driven pain ads, a long educational VSL, a static born from data), then answer Q&A on winning-ad definitions, account structure, launch volume vs quality, and idea selection. Ends with LTV strategy and a Q4 cash-prize announcement.

A 20-minute breakdown of one winning Dog Friendly Co harness ad (authority hook, power words, mechanism, sound, bridge) followed by Q&A. Key process content: how they pick which ads to review (spenders first), 95-98% of ads lose, 'put intent behind every single ad' vs mindlessly testing, lean harder into an angle once a hook proves what people care about, and 'do more, test more, close the feedback loop'.

Spencer and Carlo walk through why the supplement brand Zen was stuck at ~$2k/day for three months and how going back to 'why was the product created' plus customer feedback produced new angles (loose skin, stress, weight maintenance) that immediately produced a top spender; they also break down a Grounding Well headline test and answer Q&A. The key rule for this question is the 'shifting percentage' between net-new concepts and iterations: 80-90% net new when plateaued, 80% iteration / 20% net new once a winner pops, sliding back toward net new as iteration efficiency decays.

Community Q&A covering career/agency questions, mechanisms and awareness stages, how to iterate on winners (learnings-driven net-new ads, not small tweaks), a 7-day 'is it getting spend' kill/keep rule, why media buying structure does not matter, funnel segmentation only above $5-10k/day, and mastering feedback loops (study -> research -> create -> test -> analyze) as the thing that separates those who scale. The word 'intent' is never used in this part.

Community Q&A call (Carlo + Laura) mostly about careers: Upwork vs job board, proving value when applying, onboarding strategists, outsourcing vs going deep with one brand, and a live review of a supplement ad. Contains a few directly relevant passages: the 80/20 'sliding' ratio between new concepts and iterations, how to judge a high-spend ad below KPI, when a losing ad is worth reiterating, landing-page testing inside the main campaign, and 'close the feedback loop'.

Live Q&A (Carlo, with Spencer at the end). Core content for this question: the 'sliding technique' (80% new swings when nothing works, 80% iterations once a winner exists, drifting to 50-50 as the angle desaturates), a seven-item iteration playbook for a scaled winner (extend problem section, in media res, overcome objections, text-on-screen, static/native, congruent landing page), spent-but-no-purchase = execution problem, and the diagnosis that an ad dying fast means it only reached bottom-of-funnel/warm people and needs more emotion to convert cold audiences. Rest is career/agency/Upwork advice.

Community Q&A call: mostly productivity, pricing, career and bounty-platform questions. Contains a few ad-relevant answers: volume only matters once you scale (below ~1k/day you do not need much volume), team learnings calls review every tested ad, CPMs are ignored if the ad is profitable, losing-but-high-CTR ads should be iterated toward more emotion, and the one direct use of 'intent': submit fewer high-intent ads, don't spam random ones, wait for feedback and make data-driven decisions.

Weekly Q&A: first half is a guest interview with Konstantinos (editor turned creative strategist) about his journey, workflow for a new brand (research, account winners/graveyard, iterations) and pricing; second half is community Q&A covering how long to iterate a winner, kill/keep metrics (spend and KPI first, soft metrics second), testing angles in parallel, doing learnings as a team, A/B testing simple vs complex narratives, and the explicit rule that at $1k/day you need at most five new concepts per week.

Live team learnings call reviewing five Dog Friendly Co ad bounties (one 150k+ winner, several 'showed potential but died' ads, one static). Ends with Q&A that states the team's weekly cadence (3-5 batches = 9-15 ads per brand per week, chosen by 'highest intent'), why they don't spam creatives, and a plea for at least 1 in 10 ads to be a genuinely new angle instead of a copy of the current winners.

Intro to the Ecomtalent AI sub-program: three sections (AI images, AI videos, AI workflows), an Old Spice example product, consistent AI humans, unlimited B-roll, and a fully AI-generated UGC ad. Stresses attention to detail so AI content does not look sloppy.

Timeline of generative AI in ecom from Feb 2024 (product-on-background composites) through ChatGPT-4o, Arcads, Nano Banana, Veo and Sora 2 to Oct 2025. Concludes that one-click ad automations are mostly garbage today, manual model-combining plus taste wins, and that AI ads work only if they respect human psychology.

Short tool overview: Google (Nano Banana, Veo) and OpenAI (GPT image, Sora 2) as leaders, use official prompting docs and the vendor's own chat model to write prompts, Higgsfield vs pay-as-you-go fal.ai.

fynd.citat: you can't judge an ads performance in just day or two. That's why we do something that's called testing. We have to test all of our ads. And typically, you need to let ads run for at least three to seven days before you can tell if they're working or not,
fynd.poang: Every ad is tested and needs 3-7 days of data before it can be judged a winner or loser.

fynd.citat: I've seen ads that looked terrible on day one, but ended up crushing it by day five. And I've also seen ads that start strong, but die off completely. And that's why media buyers usually let ads run for about a week before deciding if they're winners or losers, unless they're obviously burning money from the start.
fynd.poang: Kill/keep decisions are made after about a week, with an exception for ads that obviously burn money from the start.

fynd.citat: for direct response advertising to work your ads Really have to be on point you can't just throw any random add out and expect it to work you need to send the right message to the right person at the exact right time
fynd.poang: Quality over random volume: each ad must carry the right message to the right person at the right time, not be thrown at the wall.

fynd.citat: You can run ads for 10 20 50 hundred bucks a day and third and this is the best part It gives you instant feedback your ads either work or they don't work
fynd.poang: Direct response works at any budget and gives instant, measurable feedback on whether an ad works.

fynd.citat: It's held a lot cheaper to you know test and iterate with and the key when making ads is actually staying open-minded and Just letting the data guide you like test both and if one works better than the other that's great You just learn that right
fynd.poang: Raw content is cheaper to test and iterate with; test both styles and let data decide rather than following a fixed rule.

fynd.citat: never get so caught up in in one rule like marketing and advertising is always evolving and What works today might not work tomorrow and that's why we need to you know constantly adapt constantly trying new stuff
fynd.poang: Do not lock into one rule; constantly adapt and try new things because what works changes.

fynd.citat: They upload the ads in the ad account, they run them, then they monitor performance, see if the ad is doing well. If it's not doing well, if it's doing well, they push it a bit more, you know, they give it more spend.
fynd.poang: Testing loop: winners get more spend, non-performers are switched off.

fynd.citat: we have an ad that's, you know, running for seven days and it's absolutely crushing, it has good performance, like it has good metrics, it's profitable. We try to look at it and understand, okay, why is this doing so well? How can we replicate that
fynd.poang: Iteration starts from a profitable seven-day winner: understand why it works and replicate that success in the next ads.

fynd.citat: if an ad was running for, I don't know, five days and it didn't get any purchases, it just wasted money, we obviously shut it down. And then we try to figure out why this ad didn't work. So we can avoid doing the same mistakes in our future ads.
fynd.poang: Losers (no purchases after ~5 days) are shut down and analysed so the mistake is not repeated.

fynd.citat: So this is where we analyze what worked and what didn't. We look at where people dropped off. We maybe read some comments on the ads, reactions on the ads.
fynd.poang: Iteration analysis uses drop-off points, comments and reactions, not just purchase metrics.

fynd.citat: And at this stage, we just want to kind of generate as much ideas as possible for the product that we're working for. Next comes strategy. Basically strategy is like doing brainstorming, but in a more structured way, you're actually thinking about, okay, could this idea work?
fynd.poang: Volume belongs in brainstorming; strategy then filters ideas so only the ones judged likely to work go to copywriting and production.

fynd.citat: And you have the opportunity to just find an ad and do the same ad for your brand. And I wanna explain why that's bad because when you do that, you can only be second best in the market because you're copying other brands.
fynd.poang: Copying competitor ads one-to-one caps you at second best; new concepts should come from research, not from cloning spy-tool ads.
